title: How much does a trip to Egypt cost? A full budget breakdown
summary: A trip to Egypt costs less than most bucket-list destinations once flights are booked. See the full budget by travel style. Compare and start saving.
body_markdown:
Egypt has a reputation as a fairly cheap destination for travellers, and in some ways it earns that reputation. A plate of koshari costs a few dollars, and a metro ride costs well under one. The surprises come from everything else: site tickets, internal travel, guides, and a Nile cruise. When you add it all up, a week-long trip to Egypt can cost from a few hundred dollars to several thousand per person, depending on how you travel.


This guide breaks it down line by line, using prices checked at the time of publishing so you can build a budget that fits you. Figures are in US dollars per person and exclude international flights unless stated otherwise.


A one-week trip to Egypt typically costs between $360 per person on a tight budget and $2,200 or more for a comfortable one, excluding flights. The main costs are accommodation, internal travel or a Nile cruise, site entry tickets, guides and food. Entry tickets can take a bigger share of the budget than many travellers expect.


## How much does a trip to Egypt cost in total?


A week in Egypt costs roughly $360 to $800 per person on a budget, $870 to $1,580 at mid-range, and $2,230 to $4,280 for a comfortable trip, excluding international flights. Those are estimates for November 2026, and your own total will land wherever your choices put it.


Here’s the Egypt travel budget by travel style, for seven days:


Cost line (per person, 7 days) Budget Mid-range Comfortable


Accommodation $100–$250 $350–$600 $1,050–$2,100


Food and drink $70–$140 $140–$280 $350–$600


Internal travel $50–$150 $150–$250 $250–$500


Site entry tickets $80–$150 $120–$220 $200–$350


Guides, drivers and tips $30–$80 $80–$200 $350–$700


Visa $30 $30 $30


Total $360–$800 $870–$1,580 $2,230–$4,280


‍


A few notes on reading it:


- **Budget** means hostels or guesthouses, street food, public transport, and a self-guided approach with a few paid extras.
- **Mid-range** means three- or four-star hotels, casual restaurants, a domestic flight or sleeper train, and a guide on some days.
- **Comfortable** means four- or five-star hotels, nicer restaurants, flights between cities, and private guides or drivers.
- **A Nile cruise isn’t in these totals.** It replaces some hotel nights and meals, so it gets its own section below.


The ranges come from tour operator and travel guide estimates checked in November 2026, so treat them as a planning guide, not a quote.


## Flights, transfers and internal travel


For most travellers from the US, the flight to Cairo is the single biggest cost, and round-trip fares typically range from $620 to $1,100 per person. Where you land in that range depends on your departure city, the airline, and how many stops you’re willing to make.


Timing matters too. One fare tracker’s November 2026 data showed January and February as the cheapest months to fly from the US, but hotel rates tend to climb around Christmas and New Year. Compare a few date combinations before you book.


Once you’re in Egypt, most itineraries follow the Nile: Cairo, then Luxor, then Aswan. Here’s what these usually cost:


- **Domestic flights, Cairo to Luxor or Aswan:** Roughly $50 to $150 one way. Fares swing a lot by date and how early you book.
- **Overnight sleeper train, Cairo to Luxor or Aswan:** Roughly $90 to $130 per person. It also saves you a night at a hotel.
- **Private driver for a day:** Often quoted at $50 to $100 in tour operator guides, usually for a day of sightseeing in one city.


Airport transfers and local rides are small next to these, but they add up over a week, so keep a little aside for them.


### How much does a Nile cruise cost?


A three- to four-night Nile cruise between Luxor and Aswan typically costs about €400 to €850 per person on a budget or standard five-star ship, and roughly €850 to €3,250 on deluxe and luxury ones. Those figures are quoted in euros and are based on double occupancy, meaning you share a cabin.


The fare usually covers your cabin and all meals, and on many ships, a shared guide and sightseeing transport. Some costs are often extra, so check the inclusions before you compare prices:


- Temple entry fees, quoted at about €65 per person
- Crew tips, quoted at about €20 per night
- Drinks and Wi-Fi
- Add-ons such as an Abu Simbel trip, quoted at about €100


A cruise replaces some of your hotel nights and meals, so don’t add the full fare on top of the budget table above without taking those out.


## Accommodation and food


Accommodation is usually your highest day-to-day cost, and nightly rates in Egypt range from about $15 at the budget end to $600 or more at the top end. Tour operator guides checked in November 2026 put typical rates like this:


- **Budget:** About $15 to $35 a night for hostels, guesthouses and simple hotels
- **Mid-range:** About $50 to $120 a night for three- and four-star hotels
- **Comfortable and luxury:** About $150 to $600 a night for four- and five-star hotels and resorts


The budget table earlier assumes the lower to middle part of each range, which is where many travellers end up when they also spend a night on a train or a Nile ship. Rates rise in peak season, roughly late November to February, so the same room can cost noticeably more around Christmas and New Year. If you want a sense of what everyday prices look like for people who live there, the[cost of living in Cairo](https://grey.co/blog/cost-of-living-in-cairo) is a useful reference.


Food is where Egypt is genuinely cheap, if you eat the way locals do. Typical prices from the same guides:


- **Street food and local eateries:** About $2 to $8 a meal, and as little as $3 to $7 in budget guides
- **Casual sit-down restaurants:** About $10 to $20 a meal in some guides, and $15 to $35 for mains in others
- **Upmarket restaurants:** About $25 to $50 a meal


In the table, food works out to around $10 to $20 a day on a budget, $20 to $40 at mid-range, and $50 to $85 for a comfortable trip. That assumes a mix of cheap meals and a few proper sit-down ones. Eating every meal at hotel restaurants or tourist-facing places near the major sites will push you well above these figures.


## Site entry tickets and guides


Egypt entry fees for the main sites add up to roughly $90 to $120 per person, and most visitors spend more once they add extra tombs and temples. The biggest single-ticket attraction is the Grand Egyptian Museum, which will cost $35 for foreign adult visitors from 1 November 2026.


Here are the major sites in US dollars. Sources disagree on several of these, so they’re shown as ranges:


Two cautions apply. First, ticket prices are revised regularly, so check the current price on the official ticketing channel before you travel. Second, tickets are priced in Egyptian pounds, so the dollar figure moves with the exchange rate. The table uses a rate of about 53-54 pounds per dollar as of mid-November 2026.


The table doesn’t include everything. Extra tombs in the Valley of the Kings are ticketed separately, and sites such as Philae and Hatshepsut’s temple cost more again. That’s why the site entry line in the budget table runs higher than the total here.


On guides: you can visit most sites on your own, and many travellers do. A private driver is often quoted at $50 to $100 per day, and a licensed guide is usually arranged as well. Guide fees vary, so ask what’s included before you agree. Tips are separate: tour operator guides suggest budgeting about $5 to $10 a day.


One more fixed cost is your visa. A single-entry e-visa costs $30, rising to $33 from 1 January 2027, and a visa on arrival is currently $30. Check Egypt’s official visa portal to confirm what applies to your passport before you book.


## Money, cards and currency in Egypt


The simplest way to handle money in Egypt is a mix: Egyptian pounds (EGP) in cash for markets, tips, taxis and small cafés, and a card for hotels, larger restaurants, malls and many ticket offices.


Start with the exchange rate, because it affects every other number in this guide. In mid-November 2026, it was about 53-54 to the US dollar, and it has been moving. Before you go,[convert your budget into Egyptian pounds](https://grey.co/convert) at the current rate, then check again a few days before you fly.


A few practical points on Egypt currency exchange:


- **Cash limits:** Egypt limits how much local currency you can carry in or out of the country, currently EGP 5,000 per person, and you must declare foreign currency worth more than $10,000. Check the latest customs rules before you travel.
- **ATMs:** Cash machines in cities and tourist areas are the usual way to top up on pounds. The local bank and your own bank may each charge a withdrawal fee, and some machines cap how much you can take out at once, so ask your bank before you go and withdraw larger amounts less often.
- **Dynamic currency conversion:** If a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in US dollars instead of Egyptian pounds, decline and pay in pounds. That offer is called dynamic currency conversion, and the rate it applies is usually less favourable than the one you get by paying in local currency.
- **Cash for small spending:** Markets, street food, tips and many taxis are cash-based, so don't count on cards for everything.

## Frequently asked questions


### How much does a week in Egypt cost?


A week in Egypt costs about $360 to $800 per person on a budget, $870 to $1,580 at mid-range, and $2,230 to $4,280 for a comfortable trip, excluding international flights. Add roughly $620 to $1,100 for a round-trip flight from the US, and remember that a Nile cruise replaces some hotel and food costs rather than adding to them.


### Is Egypt cheap for tourists?


Egypt is cheap for food, local transport and basic accommodation, but not for everything. Site entry tickets, internal flights, guides, and cruises cost real money, and for many visitors, they make up a larger share of the budget than the daily basics do.


### How much cash should you take to Egypt?


Carry enough for tips, markets, taxis and small cafés, and top up from ATMs as you go. One tour operator’s budget guide suggests $50 to $70 a day if you rely on cash for most spending, and you’ll need far less if you pay by card at hotels and larger restaurants. Remember the limit of EGP 5,000 in local currency that you can carry in or out of the country.


### Do you need a guide for the pyramids?


No. You can buy a ticket for the Giza Plateau and explore on your own, and many visitors do. A guide mostly adds history and context, so if you hire one, agree on the price and what it includes before you start.


### What is the cheapest month to visit Egypt?


For flights from the US, one fare tracker’s November 2026 data showed January and February as the cheapest months. Hotel prices are usually lowest in the hot summer months, roughly June to August, though temperatures in Luxor and Aswan are very high then. Many travellers consider the cooler months from around October to April the best time to visit Egypt for sightseeing, but that’s also when prices peak, especially around Christmas and New Year.


### Are cards widely accepted in Egypt?


Cards are accepted at hotels, upmarket restaurants, malls and many ticket offices, but markets, street food stalls, small cafés and many taxis are mostly cash. Carry some Egyptian pounds, and if a terminal offers to charge you in dollars, choose pounds instead.
